Incorporating backtracking yields an anytime method that returns the best feasible solution found when interrupted, or can be run as a complete search to return and certify the optimum. For suitable single-variable or pairwise reductions, an initial IQO path can determine the branching schedule without further quantum calls, though certifying the optimum may take superpolynomial classical time. To motivate our framework, we prove two limitations of irreversible IQO reductions based on the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). We show an infinite family of unweighted MaxCut instances on which globally optimized level-1 QAOA makes standard Recursive QAOA strictly prefer a first reduction that excludes every optimal solution, and limits that branch to an approximation ratio of at most $2/3+o(1)$. In contrast, a single backtrack recovers an optimal solution using the same quantum information. Causal cone arguments give a complementary obstruction at every fixed depth of standard QAOA: a weighted MaxCut instance is shown to contain two edges with identical two-qubit reduced states, even though every optimum requires opposite edge parities. MaxCut experiments show that QAOA-guided ordering is nonrandom in exact-certification tests through $n=28$, while demonstrating that quantum samples can strengthen the incumbent and enable further pruning. Our results suggest that quantum data could provide useful guidance toward solving hard combinatorial optimization problems more effectively than either quantum or classical algorithms alone.

papers.title: Coherence controls the visibility of frozen disorder in an open quantum chain
papers.summary: A Gaussian position distribution need not imply that frozen disorder is irrelevant. We study a resonant quantum chain where neighboring sites couple with opposite signs to auxiliary states that decay with frozen, random return probabilities. Lowering dephasing spreads the effect of each local return bias over more sites. We take dephasing to zero at a fixed, sufficiently weak disorder amplitude. On the scale of a coherent wave packet, the position distribution approaches the same Gaussian for almost every frozen sample. At larger distances and later times, it remains sample dependent and is described by diffusion in a random potential with Brownian spatial statistics. The covariance of bounded, direction-sensitive position readouts from independent trials in the same field distinguishes these regimes. Simulations resolve their separation at finite dephasing. Taking weak disorder before vanishing dephasing also reveals a different packet-scale response from a memoryless random-force model matched in clean diffusion and leading potential strength. The coherent response develops an integrable logarithmic peak near the initial site, where the reference response stays finite. It reflects the correlated duration and displacement of motion between jumps, together with the unfinished packet at measurement.

papers.title: State Synthesis with an NP oracle
papers.summary: In this note, I describe a quantum algorithm that prepares an arbitrary state $|\psi\rangle$ to inverse exponential precision in polynomial time by making queries to an $\mathsf{NP}$ oracle, assuming one can directly query entries of the state vector corresponding to $|\psi\rangle$. The previous best upper bound on the complexity class required by an oracle for this task was $\mathsf{PP}$. I provide evidence that $\mathsf{NP}$ is the best possible upper bound by showing that any quantum algorithm using a $\mathsf{P}$ oracle, or even a $\mathsf{P/poly}$ oracle, requires exponentially many queries. I also discuss some implications of this result for the $\mathsf{QMA}$ search-to-decision problem and unitary synthesis.

papers.title: Spin SYK-dot chains: entanglement bound and resource estimates towards a quantum advantage
papers.summary: Ground states of Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK)-type models are volume-law entangled, which makes them costly both for tensor networks and for quantum hardware simulations. Thus, it remains unclear where quantum hardware could outperform classical simulation of such models. In this work, we study a spin SYK-dot chain, in which q dense SYK dots of p qubits are joined by single ZZ bonds of strength K. The entanglement across any cut is then bounded by floor(p/2) ln 2 plus the inter-dot entanglement, and the two-qubit depth of one Trotter step is set by p alone. A resource estimate shows that a quantum advantage for the ground state could appear only for dots of about 15 to 21 qubits or more. There, a single Trotter step already requires two-qubit error rates of order 10^{-6}, beyond the reach of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. We test the assumptions of this estimate with an imaginary-time matrix product state (MPS) that applies each dot as one block. It agrees with exact diagonalisation at (p, q) = (6, 2). At (5, 2), a variational circuit with the same dot-plus-link layout comes within 3.6% of the exact energy, and noisy simulations show that its fidelity decays as assumed in the resource estimate. At (8, 5), i.e., N = 40 qubits, the energy converges at bond dimension chi = 768, far below the exact value 2^20, and the inter-dot entanglement stays small and is set mainly by K. Out-of-time-order correlators across the links decay on a time scale that shrinks rapidly with |K|. Thus, the dot size p and the inter-dot coupling K together set the entanglement of the chain, and with it where a quantum advantage could appear.

papers.title: Qyantram: A Transparent and Verifiable Quantum Computing Platform
papers.summary: Most quantum circuit platforms focus on idealized circuit assembly and simulation, hiding hardware compilation, error identification, and variational model training behind black-box operations. QYANTRAM addresses this gap through an open platform comprising four subsystems, built around evidence-backed results and independent verification. Its staged compilation pipeline makes every transformation traceable, while the router publishes rejected SWAP candidates and their scores for transparent decision-making. Verification exploits inactive qubits remaining in the |0> state, reducing complexity from 2^N to 2^k for k active qubits. This mathematically exact reduction enables full pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts, achieving approximately 10,000x speed-ups with execution times below one millisecond. The error identification engine exhaustively evaluates all Pauli error patterns without sampling, matching closed-form predictions within 2.8e-17. Its machine-learning engine achieves numerical agreement within 2.0e-15 of qiskit.quantum_info while training 25-50 times faster. The router introduces approximately 1.27x more SWAP gates than Qiskit's SABRE due to its omission of optimization, trading routing efficiency for complete decision transparency and traceability.

papers.title: Quartet state of the neutral nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond and optimized spin readout under near-infrared two-photon excitation
papers.summary: Photoionization of the excited nitrogen-vacancy center (NV-) in diamond leaves the neutral defect in a metastable quartet state of unknown energy. Using two-photon optically detected magnetic resonance with a tunable femtosecond laser, we resolve its onset in the spin contrast at 1.23 +/- 0.02 eV and, with the ground-state threshold from the same setup, place the quartet 0.54 +/- 0.04 eV above the neutral ground state. The threshold sets the optimum excitation for spin readout at 1060-1075 nm, in the near-infrared tissue window, with 26-37% higher shot-noise-limited sensitivity than at 1030-1040 nm.

papers.title: High-fidelity non-adiabatic dark state gates for neutral atoms
papers.summary: Rydberg blockade gates are the most experimentally mature entangling operations in neutral-atom quantum processors, combining fast gate times with simple control, but their performance degrades at larger interatomic separations and remains sensitive to motional and technical noise. Non-blockade gate schemes, such as dark state and geometric protocols, offer complementary robustness but typically rely on complex and experimentally demanding control. Here we show that quantum optimal control enables non-blockade gate schemes to be implemented using the experimentally established pulse-shaping techniques developed for blockade-based gates. Focusing on the dark state gate, we construct non-adiabatic implementations that preserve the intrinsic robustness of adiabatic dark state protocols while achieving gate times comparable to time-optimal blockade gates using only smooth, experimentally feasible pulses. The resulting gates exhibit enhanced resilience to motional coupling, laser noise, and interaction inhomogeneity, particularly near and beyond the blockade radius. This work establishes a practical route to fast, robust non-blockade-based two-qubit gates without increased experimental complexity.

papers.title: Weak-coupling selection and finite-torus entropy in the triangular Ising antiferromagnet
papers.summary: An antiferromagnetic second-neighbor interaction favors stripe order in the triangular-lattice Ising antiferromagnet, but uniform stripes cannot satisfy odd periodic boundaries. At each fixed odd size $L\geq5$, we minimize this interaction over the ground states of the zero-field nearest-neighbor model on an $L\times L$ torus. We prove a minimum total interface length of $4L$ and classify all $L^2(L^2-1)/2$ selected states. Under the uniform measure on these states, the area fractions of the three stripe orientations approach a uniform distribution over all nonnegative triples summing to one. Thus selection reduces an exponential degeneracy to polynomial growth, while the whole-sample orientation fractions remain broadly distributed. We also derive explicit two-sided entropy-density bounds for periodic spin ground states and honeycomb dimer coverings on $M\times N$ tori, where $M,N$ are the periods along the two primitive lattice directions. For all $M,N\geq3$, the errors relative to the bulk residual entropy are bounded by explicit constants times $\min(M,N)^{-2}$, without an aspect-ratio restriction. These bounds give finite-size accuracy guarantees and control the exponentially small fraction of unperturbed ground states that survive the selection.

papers.title: Disorder, Interactions, and the Fate of the Two-Dimensional Electron System: Wigner Crystal, Metal-Insulator Transition, and Amorphous Solid
papers.summary: We present a unified theoretical study of the interplay between Coulomb disorder and Coulomb interactions in two-dimensional electron systems, covering the Wigner crystallization transition, the metal-insulator transition, and the crossover from a Wigner crystal to an amorphous localized solid in both zero magnetic field and the lowest Landau level. Using Hartree-Fock theory, variational Monte Carlo, and percolation and strong-localization arguments, we show that quenched charged disorder destroys true long-range Wigner crystalline order in the thermodynamic limit at any nonzero charged-impurity density, within the Imry-Ma-Larkin framework; the finite-system density image is that of an amorphous solid with crystalline coherence over at most a few lattice spacings. For the two-dimensional metal-insulator transition we show, in a controlled nonlinear-Thomas-Fermi model of long-range Coulomb disorder at setback d, that the half-depletion density of the semiclassical landscape and the Ioffe-Regel-Mott density of Born-RPA transport track each other to within a factor of order unity over the physically relevant range of impurity density and setback, with a slow n_i^(-1/10) d^(-1/5) spread; the agreement reflects the common energy scale E_dis ~ E_F at the transition rather than a theorem, and modest independent short-range transport channels can shift the ratio by factors of order two. The article is a theoretical study under well-defined approximations; it takes the recent scanning tunneling microscopy imaging experiments on two-dimensional electron systems and the longstanding disorder-versus-interaction debate on the two-dimensional metal-insulator transition as motivation, and leaves to the reader the comparison between its calculated signatures and the published experimental analyses.

papers.title: Theory of Berry Singularity Markers: Diagnosing Topological Phase Transitions via Lock-In Tomography
papers.summary: This work brings forward an alternative approach for inferring the topological character of phase transitions in insulators. The method relies on subjecting the system of interest to a set of external fields which consist of two parts, i.e., a weak spatiotemporally slowly-varying component on top of a constant offset. This process maps the Berry singularities dictating the bulk band structure of the insulator to a synthetic space spanned by the control parameters of the external fields. By measuring the response of the system to the weak part of the perturbations, when these are additionally chosen to form spacetime textures, one can construct a quantity that is here-termed Berry singularity marker (BSM). The BSM enables the Berry singularity detection as it becomes nonzero only in the close vicinity of a Berry singularity and is equal to its charge. Moreover, near the Berry singularities, the BSM encodes the quantum metric tensor of the system. An advantage of the present method is that it can be implemented in a lock-in fashion, thus allowing to ``filter out'' disorder effects, therefore opening the door to the resilient diagnosis of topological phase transitions.

papers.title: Channel Estimation for Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces with Mutual Coupling
papers.summary: Channel estimation for stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIMs) has relied on the cascade model, which ignores mutual coupling and inter-layer reflection. Under a coupling-consistent multiport model, we show that the pilots are linear in the unknown channel segments and derive least-squares and linear minimum-mean-square-error estimators, an identifiability condition and an exact error decomposition for the reactance training schedule, and a gradient-based schedule design. Cascade-based estimation floors above $0$~dB normalized error at practical layer spacings and collapses the sum rate below that of the bare feed, whereas the proposed estimators retain about $80\%$ of the perfect-channel-knowledge sum rate.

papers.title: Ranking the Parameters Shaping Grid Dynamics
papers.summary: Generator and transmission line parameters do not shape the time-domain behavior of a power system equally; a parameter that dominates one dynamic property can be almost invisible to another. This paper studies how the physical parameters of a detailed and general nonlinear differential algebraic equation (DAE) grid model shape the properties that decide whether system states such as frequencies, voltages, and angles can be inferred, observed, controlled, and kept stable. The rankings are conditional as they depend on where grid sensors and actuators sit, on the operating region and the disturbance, on the network topology, and on other settings that the operator chooses. The framework combines DAE trajectory sensitivities, variational Gramians, and stability margin sensitivities to measure how much each parameter reshapes the network dynamics. On three benchmark systems, the rankings show where dynamic leverage concentrates and where the control-theoretic metrics disagree, and they point to how parameter studies can guide calibration, sensor and actuator placement, and security assessment. The proposed methods herein are also scalable and can be tested on grids with tens of thousands of buses.

papers.title: Clock Offsets and Ranges from Optical Pseudoranges
papers.summary: This note describes the estimation of ranges and clock offsets from measured pseudoranges in the context of the Kepler Navigation System. The latter system continuously adapts the frequency of its clocks to ensure that they all show the same time independently of where they are. In Medium Earth Orbits, the joint problem of estimating ranges and clock offsets can then be factorized.

papers.title: Charge-Balanced Control of Linear Systems: Controllability, Stabilizability, and Periodic Regulation
papers.summary: Electrical neuromodulation is a therapeutic approach that regulates neural activity by delivering electrical currents to brain tissue to treat brain disorders, such as epilepsy and Parkinson's disease. A critical safety requirement is charge balance, which ensures zero net injected charge over each stimulation cycle. Despite its clinical importance, the implications of charge-balanced stimulation for system dynamics and control remain poorly understood. This article investigates the controllability, stabilizability, and regulation of discrete-time linear systems under charge-balanced input constraints, motivated by applications in electrical neuromodulation. We introduce novel notions of charge-balanced controllability and stabilizability and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for both properties. We further demonstrate that nonzero steady states cannot be maintained under charge-balanced inputs, motivating the introduction of charge-balanced periodic orbits as alternative control targets. We characterize the conditions under which convergence to such orbits is achievable and develop optimal feedback controllers to stabilize the origin and track optimal charge-balanced periodic orbits. Finally, we validate the proposed control framework using a Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model, demonstrating successful suppression of tonic spiking and highlighting the potential of our approach for controlling nonlinear dynamical systems.

papers.title: View optimization in Computed Tomography
papers.summary: Many emerging CT imaging applications must operate with data from sparse projection angles, on the order of 10 views, such as first responder scenarios, dynamic imaging of detonation events, and flash imaging of materials under extreme conditions in high energy-density science. Few-view imaging is a data undersampling problem, that degrades tomographic reconstructions with streaks, shadows, and other aliasing artifacts, due to ill-conditioning. In few- view CT, the specific set of projection angles can strongly impact reconstruction quality, and the optimal angles depend on the object being scanned. Despite a surge of recent research, there is much to explore in this problem. We present an object-aware performance prediction framework for few-view projection datasets based on a matrix decomposition of the discretized forward model augmented with expected object gradient information. The method yields a quantitative score for a candidate set of view angles that can underpin a view selection recommendation algorithm. A key feature is that it can be applied at multiple stages of acquisition: a priori, before any radiographs are taken, or adaptively, after some radiographs are collected, to determine the next best view. We demonstrate the approach using simulated CT data with 5 view and 15 view configurations. Preliminary results are encouraging; images reconstructed using a standard statistical algorithm show that reconstruction accuracy agrees with our performance score. Reconstruction accuracy was evaluated against a known ground truth using an information theoretic score. Continued testing with complex objects and multiple geometries is necessary.
